edges.effect_quant: Across randomized and observational data, alpha blockers increase orthostatic hypotension risk, though the size of that increase depends on selectivity, dose, co-prescribed antihypertensives, and timing around treatment initiation.
edges.population: older adults and middle-aged men exposed to alpha-1 blockers for urinary or cardiovascular indications
edges.mechanism: Alpha blockers reduce peripheral vascular tone and blunt the reflex vasoconstriction needed to maintain standing blood pressure. In older adults with impaired baroreflexes or polypharmacy, that hemodynamic effect can readily translate into dizziness, hypotension, syncope, and falls.
edges.summary: This is a straightforward class-harm edge. The best randomized synthesis shows alpha blockers carry increased odds of orthostatic hypotension, and older observational cohorts make the clinical consequence concrete by showing more hypotension-related events around treatment initiation.
edges.caveats: Risk varies across agents and is highest at initiation, reinitiation, dose escalation, and in people already taking other blood-pressure-lowering drugs. Uroselective agents may be safer than nonselective ones, but they do not eliminate the problem.
